companies.name: Tanzania Electric Supply Company Limited (TANESCO)
companies.role: The state-owned national electricity utility, which implemented the on-grid component directly rather than through local developers, prepared the resettlement action plan of July 2007 and its amendment of January 2014, carried out the valuations and paid the compensation. companies.name: Kurasini Oil Storage Company Limited, formerly MPS Oil (T) Limited

companies.name: Rail Assets Holding Company (RAHCO)
companies.role: The state body that then held Tanzania's railway land. TANESCO was allowed to put its new 132 kV line inside 30 metres of the centre line of RAHCO's railway wayleave at Ukonga, and because the land belonged to RAHCO the affected people were paid for improvements on the land only and not for the land (Amendment of Resettlement Action Plan, January 2014).

tedap-ukonga-mzinga-wayleaves.community: The project rebuilt transmission and distribution lines and substations in Dar es Salaam, Moshi and Arusha, and the wayleaves it needed ran through built-up suburbs. The completion report says changing the wayleave in the densely populated suburbs of Dar es Salaam was costly and slowed the works, and that no additional resettlement plans were prepared for resettlements that had not been foreseen. A resettlement audit the Bank commissioned in September 2017, shortly before closing, put the number of project-affected people under the on-grid component at 11,070. The audit concluded that the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy had been followed, though implementation tended to conform more closely to Tanzanian law and practice than to the Bank's standards, and that poor recordkeeping of resettlement activities impeded effective monitoring of resettlement and its impact. TANESCO's own amendment to the resettlement plan, dated January 2014, gives the detail. At Ukonga, where the new 132 kV line was routed within 30 metres of the centre line of the railway wayleave from the Factory Zone II substation at Gongo la Mboto to the Factory Zone III substation at Kipawa, it names 43 affected people one by one and what each lost. The entries against the names read, in the amendment's own words: part of house, part of uncompleted house, part of the house, part of house affected, part of the house and septic tank affected, part of house and toilet affected, fence and house, and in one case '75% of house affected, Borehole, Trees'. Many of the entries are kiosks, one of them 'Kiosk (3)'. Others are trees, sugar cane, maize, tomatoes, sweet tomatoes, cassava, pawpaw, bananas, orange and guava, vegetables, boreholes, a tank, fences, hedges and part of a foundation. The amendment publishes no totals by type of loss. The amendment describes these people as having encroached into the railway wayleave, says the Managing Director approved valuing and compensating them for exhausted improvements made on the land only, because the land belonged to the railway company, in order to meet the Bank's requirement and allow the contractor to continue with works smoothly, and records that the compensation paid came to Tshs 300,639,109.92. It states that these people were compensated so as to allow the contractor to proceed with the construction, and that at a meeting on 18 September 2011 at Ukonga Magereza the affected people asked TANESCO to pay for their property excluding land and to give them enough time to vacate, and asked that the actual end of the 30-metre corridor be demarcated before the final counting of the properties to be compensated. TANESCO's own comment on that request reads: 'Experience shows that after compensation payment even if you give them a year PAPs are normally slow to vacate freely; a close follow up will be needed.' At Kurasini, three families in two houses were first consulted and earmarked for compensation for the substation and its wayleave; the amendment says it was later established that those people had sold their land to a company, MPS Oil (T) Limited, since renamed Kurasini Oil Storage Company Limited, and the Tshs 1,638,111,700 compensation was negotiated with and paid to that company. At Mbagala, three named individuals agreed in a meeting on 13 June 2012 to give up their plots if compensated, valuation was completed and signed by the Chief Government Valuer and a payment schedule was sent to the District Commissioner at Temeke, but the plots were then not used because another site was provided, and the amendment does not say whether those three were paid. At Mzinga Creek, a last-minute change to the design of the Kurasini to Ubungo line required a new corridor and affected 16 households. The completion report says compensation had been made for 13 of the 16 and not for 3, and that TANESCO was working on the paperwork; it says TANESCO approved a top-up compensation payment after the project was completed. The report's own lessons include that land acquisition and compensation should be completed before a project's effective date, and that a project should start immediately after compensation to avoid encroachers.
tedap-ukonga-mzinga-wayleaves.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,351 for the GEF grant P092154, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own figures are different again: the September 2017 resettlement audit put project-affected people under the on-grid component at 11,070, the January 2014 resettlement plan amendment names 43 affected people at Ukonga, and the completion report counts 16 affected households at Mzinga Creek. No document found gives a count of people actually relocated.
tedap-ukonga-mzinga-wayleaves.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the completion report, the Independent Evaluation Group's review or the resettlement plan amendment.
tedap-ukonga-mzinga-wayleaves.outcome: The credits closed on 29 September 2017 with compensation outstanding for 3 of the 16 households at Mzinga Creek; the completion report says TANESCO approved a top-up payment after the project was completed and before the report was finished. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says the completion report could usefully have provided an update on whether the compensation pending for the three remaining households at closing, nearly a year before the review, had been paid, and gives no such update. The Bank also cancelled four distribution packages over shortcomings in the bidding process and, after an inquiry by its Integrity Vice Presidency, imposed a sanction of debarment on two private companies that had submitted false financial documents in bids for project contracts. The 13 km Ubungo to Kurasini section could not be built under the project because a road expansion by the national roads authority affected the wayleave, and TANESCO was financing it with its own funds after closing.

tedap-ukonga-mzinga-wayleaves.confidence_note: The 43 named affected people at Ukonga, the amounts paid, the Kurasini and Mbagala sequences and the Managing Director's decision to pay for improvements only all come from TANESCO's own amendment to the project's resettlement plan, published by the Bank in January 2014. The 11,070 affected people, the 16 households at Mzinga Creek and the 3 left unpaid come from the Bank's completion report, which reports the findings of a resettlement audit the Bank itself commissioned; the audit report was not found. The lender and the implementing agency are therefore reporting on their own project and no independent account of these wayleaves was found. The amendment gives no totals by type of loss, and none has been worked out from its list here. No document found says what happened to the three families at Kurasini after their land was bought by the oil storage company, whether the three Mbagala landowners were paid, or whether the three Mzinga Creek households finally received the top-up. The resettlement audit concluded that the Bank's resettlement policy had been followed. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date on its pages; the 18 October 2018 date is the Bank's catalogue field for the document and is unverified at document level.
tedap-ukonga-mzinga-wayleaves.conditions: The project was environmental category B and triggered six safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, physical cultural resources, involuntary resettlement, safety of dams, and projects on international waterways. An environmental and social impact assessment was prepared in 2005 for the on-grid transmission lines and an environmental audit was done at the substations to be upgraded; TANESCO updated the assessment and the documents were disclosed in 2007. A resettlement action plan for the transmission lines and substations in Dar es Salaam, Moshi and Arusha was disclosed in July 2007. A resettlement policy framework and an environmental and social management framework were prepared for the off-grid component and disclosed in 2007; the Rural Energy Agency found them hard for subproject developers to use and had them rewritten by a consultant in June 2012, translated into Kiswahili and redisclosed as a revised framework and a Resettlement Management Framework. TANESCO prepared and disclosed the amendment to the resettlement plan in January 2014 to cover additional resettlement caused by civil works in Dar es Salaam. The completion report states that no additional resettlement plans were prepared for the resettlements that had not been foreseen, and the Bank commissioned a resettlement audit in September 2017 instead, ahead of closing (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 June 2018).

companies.name: Ghana Grid Company Limited (GRIDCo)

ctb-kwabenya-stone-crackers.community: The credit paid for a 330 kV transmission line from Aboadze in the west of Ghana to the Volta substation in the east, with substation works at Volta, Akosombo and Tema. The Volta River Authority's resettlement action plan of December 2004 covered a corridor 215 km long and 860 hectares in area, and recorded that 307 of the affected people gave the size of their household, which ranged from two to thirty-one people, a mean of between 5.1 and 8.6 people by district. The plan was then overtaken by the works. The Authority's addendum to it records that during construction the line had to be realigned at Amrahia, Amanfio, Teiman, Oyarifa, Kwabenya, Pokuase and Ayawaso in Greater Accra and at Kasoa and Mankesim in the Central Region, to avoid buildings that had gone up between the survey and the construction and so to avoid, in the addendum's words, huge compensation cost. The diversions lengthened the line from 215 km to 219.2 km, took the corridor from 860 hectares to 876, added eleven towers and created impacts on people the original consultation had never reached. The addendum's tally is 1,454 affected farms, 1,051 on the original line and 403 added by the diversions, and 410 buildings or structures actually condemned, 271 in Greater Accra, 136 in the Central Region and 3 in the Western Region. It says the bulk of those properties in Greater Accra were uncompleted and that the completed houses were mostly owner-occupied by relatives and dependants of the owners, that few tenants were found and none claimed, and that the period from consultation to relocation was at least three years. Separately from the property owners it counts 22 stone crackers at Kwabenya, who were excluded from the count of property owners because what they lost was the right to carry on an economic activity rather than a property right: quarry activity is not permitted inside a transmission line corridor. The addendum says most of these operators had already been moved to new areas nearby as a result of project activities and that their compensation was based on the temporary loss of income from the day of relocating and restarting, in the nature of a disturbance claim, even though they had no legal concessions or licences to operate; the entry for stone crackers in its schedule is GHc 18,968, to be paid by end of 2010. A cut-off date of 30 August 2008 was fixed for the line as a whole and a later one of 21 April 2010 agreed with the quarry operators at Kwabenya. The addendum records that the main concern of affected people in all the meetings was the timely payment of adequate compensation. The completion report says the Ghana component complied only partially with social requirements, that about 1,700 persons were affected, and that the mid-term review found the project was not in compliance with World Bank policies because construction started before compensation. The same report, rating borrower performance, calls this one of the minor failings detected at the mid-term review, 'the initiation of works without having compensated potentially affected persons', and says it was subsequently corrected. It states that by 2011 the Volta River Authority had fully settled outstanding compensation to all affected parties, including landowners and stone crackers, affected by the passage of the 330 kV line at Kwabenya. On the Benin and Togo side the report lists, among the causes of delay, recurrent cash flow difficulties at the Communaute Electrique du Benin which affected the timely disbursement of the money set aside to compensate property and people affected by the Ghana-Togo-Benin 330 kV line.
ctb-kwabenya-stone-crackers.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,454 for this project, which it describes as an estimate of people displaced taken from World Bank documents. The figure 1,454 appears in the Volta River Authority's resettlement action plan addendum as the total number of affected farms, made up of 1,051 on the original line route and 403 added by the diversions, and not as a number of people. The completion report's own figure for people is 'about 1,700 persons were affected'. The addendum separately counts 410 buildings and structures actually condemned and 22 stone crackers at Kwabenya. No document found gives a count of people actually relocated.
ctb-kwabenya-stone-crackers.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the completion report, the Independent Evaluation Group's review or the resettlement documents.
ctb-kwabenya-stone-crackers.outcome: The 330 kV lines and substations in Ghana were completed in 2009. The completion report says the Volta River Authority had fully settled outstanding compensation to all affected parties, including the landowners and stone crackers at Kwabenya, by 2011. The report rated the project's outcome Unsatisfactory, chiefly because the cross-border interconnections were not synchronised, and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed. The Benin credit ran to 30 June 2016.

ctb-kwabenya-stone-crackers.confidence_note: The finding that construction started before compensation is the Bank's own, recorded in its completion report as a mid-term review finding and repeated in the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report. The farm, structure and stone cracker counts, the diversions and the cut-off dates come from the Volta River Authority's own resettlement plan and addendum, published by the Bank. The lender and the implementing agency are therefore reporting on their own project and no independent account of this line's land acquisition was found. The completion report says that by 2011 all outstanding compensation had been fully settled, including for the stone crackers, and does not say how long any individual went unpaid, how many people were affected by the works that began before payment, or how many of the 410 condemned structures were lived in. The addendum's table of affected houses does not add up: its district rows give 226, 16 and 1 in the column for the original number of affected people and its total row gives 43 for that column, while its columns for properties on the original line and properties affected by diversion, 292 and 118, do sum to the total of 410. The addendum prints no date; the date of July 2010 is the Bank's catalogue field for the document and its own filename says April 2011, so the document-level date is unverified. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date on its pages; the 7 May 2018 date is the Bank's catalogue field and is likewise unverified at document level. The Benin and Togo cash-flow finding concerns the second phase, under a separate project number.
ctb-kwabenya-stone-crackers.conditions: The project was environmental category B and triggered two safeguard policies, environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. The Volta River Authority prepared an environmental management plan and put it in the bidding documents, and prepared a compensation and resettlement action plan dated December 2004 before implementation, later supplemented by an addendum covering the people the diversions affected. Under the plan, affected people were compensated at the Authority's valuation of crops, land and buildings, or, where they disagreed, at the figure set by an independent valuation the Authority paid for. The addendum states that the absence of title documents did not bar a claimant from payment once ownership could be ascertained and validated, that replacement cost was estimated with no depreciation deducted, and that household relocation expenses were factored in as a disturbance element. The Benin component triggered only the environmental assessment policy, because the works there were upgrades to control and communications hardware at existing substations and required no land acquisition or resettlement (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2018; Resettlement Action Plan Addendum).

The Bank's completion report refers to a single jointly engaged transmission line contractor and a single owner's engineer and names neither (Eiffage Energie Systemes company page; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 July 2019).

wapp-apl3-zagtouli-bolgatanga-deaths.community: The project built a 225 kV transmission line between Bolgatanga in northern Ghana and Ouagadougou, 171 km of it from the Zagtouli substation to the border at Dakola and Paga and 17 km from the border to the Bolgatanga 2 substation, plus substations at both ends and shield-wire supplies to 11 villages along the route. The completion report records two fatal accidents in July 2017, less than a month apart. In the first, a transmission tower gave way while a team of two workers were carrying out assembly works on it; the tower fell to the ground carrying both men, one was declared dead at the scene and the other was seriously injured and admitted to hospital. In the second, a minor drowned in a pool that had formed in the excavated tower foundations after they filled with rain water. The report puts the accidents down to a supervision gap: only one health and safety supervisor was deployed by the owner's engineer for all the construction sites, which in places were hundreds of kilometres apart, and it says the need for more supervisors on projects covering a wide area became evident when the two deaths occurred. After the accidents the Bank's team worked with SONABEL, the owner's engineer and the contractor on a twenty-point action plan, which included certifying workers who install at heights, involving community organisations and non-governmental organisations in monitoring social activities, securing all work sites with wooden barricades before starting any work, applying the compensation provisions for such cases and producing evidence of the reports and of the start of compensation, and performing the sacrificial rituals the customary authorities demanded. Separately, the report records delays in paying compensation to project-affected people, which it attributes to some people presenting incomplete documents to back their claims, which took considerable time to verify and assess, and to farmers migrating to other places in Ghana by season so that they were not always available for the asset inventory surveys and the valuation. It says the Bank could not establish how effective the grievance redress mechanism was, because the issue only surfaced late in the project when a complaint about delayed compensation was escalated, and that there was no formal mechanism in place, only a default verbal process in which traditional and local government authorities acted as go-betweens. The resettlement action plan for the Ghana section, prepared before appraisal, counted 1,166 project-affected people in 87 households across 15 communities in the Bolgatanga Municipality and the Kassena-Nankana East and Kassena-Nankana West districts, giving an average household size of 13.0, of which 8 households were headed by women. It recorded that of 150 owners of compounds and gates surveyed, 142 lived by farming, 43 also did leather work or basketry and 17 also did petty trading, and that only 17 of the 87 households had electricity and none had its own water supply. It also recorded that the corridor, 40 metres wide over the 39.3 km of line inside Ghana, would be cleared of all trees above about 1.25 metres and that if the corridor were not acquired and the affected people not resettled before clearing, the clearing would create conflict between the project promoters and the owners of the properties.
wapp-apl3-zagtouli-bolgatanga-deaths.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,166 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The same figure appears in the resettlement action plan for the Ghana section as the population of the 87 affected households at the planning stage. No document found gives a count of people actually relocated, and the completion report gives no outcome figure for the resettlement at all.
wapp-apl3-zagtouli-bolgatanga-deaths.outcome: The line was energised and the project closed on 31 December 2018. The completion report says the project led to a significant reduction in heavy fuel oil imports in Burkina Faso. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says the Bank team was late in responding and only organised a mission after both fatal accidents had happened, that the Implementation Status and Results Reports rated overall safeguard compliance Satisfactory or Moderately Satisfactory throughout, which it says did not seem justified in 2017 when the two deaths occurred or in the later years when there was still no grievance mechanism, and that the reports appeared to lack candidness in assessing safeguard compliance. A formal grievance redress mechanism for the Ghana Grid Company was established only in 2018, the final year of implementation.

wapp-apl3-zagtouli-bolgatanga-deaths.confidence_note: Both deaths, the stated cause of the supervision gap behind them, the twenty-point action plan and the compensation delays come from the Bank's own completion report, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report repeats them and adds that the Bank team responded late and that the project's own status reports lacked candidness. No press report, court record, inquest or labour inspectorate finding on either death was found, in French or in English, and no document found names either person who died, says which contractor's site each accident happened on, or says where on the 188 km of line the accidents happened. The two Bank documents disagree on the dates: the completion report says both accidents occurred in July 2017, spaced less than a month from each other, while the review says the tower collapse was in July 2017 and the drowning a month later. The claim that all compensation was completed before closing is attributed by the review to the completion report's team rather than to a document. The identification of Eiffage Energie Systemes as the line contractor rests on the company's own account of its contract; the Bank's report names no contractor. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date on its pages; the 17 June 2020 date is the Bank's catalogue field for the document and is unverified at document level. The 87 households and 1,166 people are planning figures from the Ghana section's resettlement plan, and no outcome figure for resettlement appears in either Bank document. That plan prints no date; the date of April 2011 is the Bank's catalogue field for it and is unverified at document level.
wapp-apl3-zagtouli-bolgatanga-deaths.conditions: The project was environmental category B, partial assessment, and triggered four safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. Burkina Faso and Ghana each completed an environmental and social impact assessment with an environmental and social management plan, cleared by the Bank and disclosed in both countries and at the Bank in 2011, and each prepared and consulted on a resettlement action plan before appraisal. A land acquisition and resettlement policy framework governed the subprojects; among its principles were that before construction activities started the affected people were to be compensated, that affected people should be fully informed and consulted, that no impoverishment of affected people should result, and that compensation was due for loss of land, structures, crops and other assets. Project appraisal concluded that both utilities had sufficient capacity to manage the potential negative impacts of the line and substation construction. The completion report records that this conclusion was wrong on health and safety supervision, that the Ghana Grid Company's grievance redress mechanism was not effective in recording complaints, and that no formal grievance mechanism existed until 2018 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 July 2019; Land Acquisition and Resettlement Policy Framework).

benin-iame-transmission-compensation.community: The project financed two 161 kV transmission lines in Benin, from Onigbolo to Parakou and from Sakete to Porto-Novo, together with substations and rural electrification. The appraisal document of May 2009 says these were the only parts of the project expected to have significant social impacts, and that the resettlement action plans found 123 families, about 640 people, needed to be physically resettled along the Onigbolo to Parakou route and 61 families, about 682 people, along the Sakete to Porto-Novo route; an annex to the same document puts the same two sets of figures as families who 'will need to be resettled and/or compensated'. The plans had first been prepared in 2004 and were updated in April and May 2008, and were disclosed on 21 January 2009 at the Bank and on 28 or 29 January 2009 in Benin. The completion report gives the outcome. It says most payments under the plan were made on time, that compensation for the first 50 km had been paid by October 2012, that plans were in place to begin the next phase in December 2014, and that a further 60 km of line was still unaccounted for. The Communaute Electrique du Benin assured the project team that all payments would be made by 31 December 2014 and had, in the report's words, 'encountered some resistance from those who had not received their payments'. The report then says it later became evident that the utility lacked the cash to make the payments as planned and had to seek a commercial short-term loan to cover them, and that the payments were eventually made in early 2015. Its account of what the delay did is blunter: the utility's lack of funds for the resettlement payments led to 'the to-be relocated people blocking progress on the line', and construction of the IDA-financed transmission line only began in 2016. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of the report puts the same sequence as the utility being expected to complete all payments by December 2014, failing to process them for lack of funds, and this resulting in protests from people who could not receive their compensation. In March 2018, during a supervision mission, the Bank found irregularities in the compensation of project-affected people for the transmission line and the electrification works, including 70 project-affected people who had been identified but did not show up. The client implemented an agreed action plan to close those cases, which included the utility setting aside the compensation amount for a determined period. The review puts the same finding as 70 people who did not receive their payments because they did not contact the utility. In December 2012 a Bank mission with a safeguards specialist rated safeguard implementation Moderately Satisfactory, noting that the arrangements for integrating the safeguard measures were not always followed and that studies, permits, certificates and monitoring reports were not disseminated or archived properly; semi-annual safeguard reporting only began in 2014.
benin-iame-transmission-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,249 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own planning figure is 184 families, about 1,322 people, across the two transmission lines: 123 families, about 640 people, on the Onigbolo to Parakou line and 61 families, about 682 people, on the Sakete to Porto-Novo line, from resettlement action plans first prepared in 2004 and updated in 2008. The appraisal document's main text says these families needed to be physically resettled; its annex says they would need to be resettled and/or compensated; the completion report repeats the 1,322 with the words 'resettled and/or compensated'; and the Independent Evaluation Group's review states it as 184 families consisting of 1,322 people who 'were to be resettled'. No document found gives a count of people actually relocated.
benin-iame-transmission-compensation.suppression: No arrests, evictions by force or police action are recorded in the Bank's completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group's review. Both record action the other way: the report says people awaiting payment blocked progress on the line and that the utility encountered resistance from those who had not been paid, and the review calls this protests from people who could not receive their compensation.
benin-iame-transmission-compensation.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group's review. The report records that the contractor's field workers were not paid for periods of up to six months while ownership changes were processed and went on strike.
benin-iame-transmission-compensation.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2018, three and a half years late, after the last extension was granted in part because compensation to displaced people was still pending. Compensation for the delayed stretch was paid in early 2015 and construction of the IDA-financed line began in 2016. The 70 people found uncompensated in March 2018 were dealt with under an action plan that set their money aside for a fixed period; neither Bank document says whether any of them was finally paid. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that the project team confirmed the project was in compliance with the involuntary resettlement safeguard policy at closing.

benin-iame-transmission-compensation.confidence_note: The unpaid compensation, the people blocking the line, the commercial loan the utility had to take to pay them, the 2018 finding of irregularities and the 70 people unpaid all come from the Bank's own completion report, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report is the only other source found; the lender is reporting on its own project. Searches in French and English for Beninese press, court or non-governmental reports on compensation for these two lines found nothing on this project. No document found names a single affected person, says how many people blocked the works or for how long, says how many of the 184 families were ever physically moved, or says whether the 70 people found uncompensated in 2018 were paid. The report also states that most payments under the plan were made on time and that no residual negative impacts are reported, and the review records the project team's confirmation that the project complied with the resettlement policy at closing. The appraisal document's main text and its annex describe the same 184 families in two different ways, one as needing physical resettlement and the other as needing resettlement and/or compensation, and the review drops the second half of that phrase. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date on its pages; the 1 May 2020 date is the Bank's catalogue field for the document and is unverified at document level.
benin-iame-transmission-compensation.conditions: The project was environmental category B, partial assessment, and triggered ten safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, pest management, physical cultural resources, involuntary resettlement, forests, indigenous peoples, safety of dams, projects in disputed areas and projects on international waterways. The implementing agencies prepared environmental and social impact assessments and management plans, managed by the environmental service of the Communaute Electrique du Benin, disclosed in Benin and at the Bank on 21 January 2009. Resettlement action plans for both transmission lines, first prepared in 2004 and updated in April and May 2008, were disclosed at the Bank on 21 January 2009 and in Benin on 28 or 29 January 2009, the two Bank documents giving different days. Carrying out the plans was to be financed by the Communaute Electrique du Benin, not by the credit. The rights of way for both lines avoided suburban and urban areas and sacred areas and ran mostly through agricultural land; the Independent Evaluation Group records the project team's comment that the natural habitats, physical cultural resources and forests policies had already been complied with at appraisal by avoiding protected and sacred forest areas and the sacred natural sites of fetisheurs, healers or diviners of animist cults, with the rest of the physical cultural resources policy met by a chance-find procedure during construction (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 24 September 2019; IEG ICR Review).

pakistan-edtip-crop-compensation.community: The project paid for new and upgraded grid stations, transmission lines and distribution networks across five state electricity companies. Resettlement action plans were prepared only by the companies that acquired land for grid stations, and an abbreviated plan by one more; in Lahore the Lahore Electric Supply Company acquired land from 15 affected people. The completion report says the major area of compensation was not the grid station land but crop and other losses suffered while the transmission line components were built. Those losses were handled under the companies' existing practice, which is to assess the damage after it has happened, through the patwaris or land revenue officers and local staff. The report states that in the absence of standardised guidelines and procedures for assessing losses, the common practice across all the distribution companies is to assess after the damage, that there is no clarity on the standardisation of compensation payments, and that 'the result was that compensation payments were severely and consistently delayed in the Project'. Three of the five companies, the Islamabad, Lahore and Multan companies, reported pending or outstanding payments even at the end of the project. In the case of the Islamabad company the payments were delayed for a year. The Multan company had paid 19 per cent of the compensation owed for crop losses by the end of the project. A grievance redress mechanism operated throughout, but the report says it had limited scope to address the main issue, the delays in assessing losses and awarding compensation for losses caused by the transmission lines. The project paid for social and environment cells inside each company to oversee social safeguards; the report also records that in one company the sub-divisional officer concerned acted as the assessor of compensation payments for transmission line work, and that this affected public grievances in that regard. The report says compliance with safeguards was not satisfactory in the early years because the implementing agencies and their contractors lacked experience, and that it improved gradually.
pakistan-edtip-crop-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,303 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The only count of affected people in the Bank's own completion report is the 15 people whose land the Lahore Electric Supply Company acquired. No Bank document found gives a count of people actually relocated, and the resettlement plans for the Islamabad and Multan companies that were examined give no total of affected households or structures.
pakistan-edtip-crop-compensation.killed_note: No death caused by the project is recorded in the completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group's review. The report's only fatality figures are a utility safety statistic it cites as a benefit: it says the installation of aerial bundled conductor in the Hyderabad company's network eliminated failure complaints and showed a drastic reduction in fatalities, with a footnote reading 'In FY13, HESCO reported zero public fatalities down from 18 and 11 in FY12 and FY11.' Those are counts of members of the public killed on that company's existing network before and during the works, not deaths caused by the project.
pakistan-edtip-crop-compensation.outcome: The loan and credits closed on 28 February 2014 with compensation payments still pending at three of the five companies, and with the Multan company having paid 19 per cent of what it owed for crop losses. Only 66 per cent of the planned subprojects were completed by the revised closing date and 51 per cent of the planned cost was spent. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory and Bank performance Unsatisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group agreed on both and said that improving performance on safeguards, particularly on compensation payments, remains critical to the distribution companies.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit C4367 of US$33.6 million for the Kampala Institutional and Infrastructure Development Project (P078382), approved by the Board on 6 November 2007. Original closing was 31 December 2010; after two extensions totalling three years the project closed on 31 December 2013. Project costs were US$37.10 million at appraisal. A restructuring approved on 3 December 2010 extended the closing date by 24 months and created an additional category of eligible expenditure for involuntary resettlement, because the government could no longer fully finance the project's resettlement cost; a second restructuring extended closing again from 31 December 2012. Environmental category B. The implementing agency was Kampala City Council, which became the Kampala Capital City Authority during the project. The Independent Evaluation Group's review rated outcome Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Moderate and quotes the completion report by paragraph (IEG ICR Review ICRR14588, date posted 25 February 2015).

companies.name: Kampala City Council, later the Kampala Capital City Authority
companies.role: The city government of Kampala and the project's implementing agency; in 2011 the elected City Council was replaced by the Capital City Authority, a central-government body under a minister, with an Executive Director appointed by the president. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says a lack of capacity in the Council and Authority, compounded by insufficient government funding for the resettlement compensation, led to the compensation problems, and that the body had no specialist to handle safeguard issues (IEG ICR Review, 25 February 2015).

kiidp-kampala-roads-compensation.community: The credit paid for rebuilding city roads, traffic junctions and drainage channels in Kampala together with reform of the city government. The resettlement action plan of October 2006 set out two design scenarios and recorded that under the second, which the City Council accepted for implementation, 415 entities, meaning individuals, households and businesses, were affected and 141 of them would relocate, some on the same plot and some to a wholly new site, with an extra 15 per cent on the value of the property allowed for the cost of moving. The plan's eligible categories ran from registered title holders down to licensees, those with the landowner's permission to put up a kiosk or grow seasonal crops but no legal claim, and squatters with neither legal nor customary claim. Its cut-off date was 15 April 2006. The plan set out a three-stage grievance procedure starting at the division office. For the roads it covered, it recorded that a 16-metre corridor would be used where houses were concentrated and that even so a number of houses would have to be partially demolished, and that owners of partly affected houses were worried they would be treated as encroachers in the road reserve in future if they were not resettled; on one road it noted that people would have to move for the second time, having already been moved under an earlier road project. The Independent Evaluation Group's review gives the outcome: by the project's closing date of 31 December 2013, 494 project-affected persons had been compensated and 239 persons had yet to receive compensation. It attributes most of the outstanding payments, citing the completion report's paragraph 48, to unsubstantiated claims, and says that by the time the completion report was concluded all eligible claims had been paid off. On the environmental side it records deficiencies in safeguard implementation, especially at the landfill: poor handling of the landfill acquisition with no proper due diligence before the six-acre extension land was bought, incomplete fencing around the site, reliance on a temporary operating licence for longer than expected, and a leachate monitoring and treatment system not commensurate with the national waste water treatment and discharge standard, posing health and safety risks to the public. It says all of those were resolved within a month of the project closing.
kiidp-kampala-roads-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,118 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The project's own resettlement action plan of October 2006 counted 415 affected entities, meaning individuals, households and businesses, of whom 141 were to relocate under the design the City Council adopted. The Independent Evaluation Group's review counts 494 people compensated and 239 not compensated by the closing date, 733 in all. No document found gives a count of people actually relocated.
kiidp-kampala-roads-compensation.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the Independent Evaluation Group's review.
kiidp-kampala-roads-compensation.outcome: The credit closed on 31 December 2013 with 239 people still unpaid. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says that by the time the completion report was concluded all eligible claims had been paid, attributing most of the outstanding payments to unsubstantiated claims, and rated the project's outcome Satisfactory. The Bank went on to lend for a Second Kampala Institutional and Infrastructure Development Project, approved 20 March 2014, under which an Inspection Panel case was later registered over the Lubigi drainage channel at Kawaala.

tanzania-tscp-compensation-delays.community: The project rebuilt roads, drains, bus stands, markets and landfills in eight Tanzanian local government areas. Each subproject had its own resettlement action plan, and the plans of March 2010 count what was to be taken. In Mbeya, a census of the city roads subproject found that the structures mostly affected were 75 buildings, 34 fences, 43 stands of permanent crops, 26 kiosks, 4 walls, 2 hedges, 15 stalls and one well, and that 55 people would be affected, mostly totally; all 55 were squatters living in the existing right of way, so they were not claiming land but structures and what they had built on it, 14 claiming for crops, 4 for a building only and 37 for both, and all 55 were to be compensated for their structures and moved to land the council provided in the Mdenga Namadi area. In Arusha, 279 households were to be affected by the proposed upgrading works, 136 of them owning structures and land except for 42 households at the Murriet dumpsite who were entitled to compensation for structures only, and 248 owning crops along four roads; at Urundini two households were to lose their houses and a third his incomplete house, and at the Murriet dumpsite four households owned eight commercial structures and two of the residential houses to be removed were traditional thatched msonge houses. Another plan counts 161 households to be affected by a proposed road, and another records that a 16-metre corridor would mean a number of houses being partially demolished and that owners of partly affected houses feared being treated in future as encroachers in the road reserve if they were not resettled. At Kisasa in Dodoma the assessors concluded there were no resettlement issues at the site itself but that three households faced potential relocation and about 20 farmlands needed compensation at the proposed Chidaya landfill, and that a payment of Tshs 400,000 per affected household, described as a token relief to cover transport to the new homes and six months' accommodation, had already been paid by the city development authority. The completion report gives the outcome. It says the subprojects complied with the resettlement action plans but faced challenges because the local government authorities fell short in paying compensation and because designs changed, and that 'RAP implementation was often delayed sometimes to over nine months when LGAs lacked funds for compensation of PAPs thus delaying construction activities and raising complaints by PAPs.' It says another problem arose when subproject designs changed, especially on drainage, which changed who was affected, and that remedial actions were identified in the resettlement plan completion reports. Separately it records that insufficient counterpart funding from the local authorities was an ongoing issue through the life of the project, and that acquiring land for the sanitary landfill buffer zones in Mwanza, Kigoma-Ujiji and Mbeya and the road corridor wayleaves for Ilemela and Arusha all had periods when implementation was delayed for want of counterpart funds, despite repeated engagement between the Bank, the local authorities, the President's Office and the Treasury. It adds that delay in utility removal and compensation was revealed to be a source of grievances. Grievance handling committees were set up in all subproject areas and kept logbooks, but the report says the project included no grievance procedure at contractor level, which could have helped resolve and monitor complaints by workers, and that the grievance mechanism as a whole was characterised by a lack of funds because its activities were never budgeted at project design, leaving the committees' survival after closing uncertain.
tanzania-tscp-compensation-delays.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,054 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The project's own subproject resettlement plans of March 2010 count planned impacts city by city, including 279 households in Arusha, 161 households on another road, 55 squatters in Mbeya and three households facing relocation at the Chidaya landfill near Dodoma. The completion report gives no count of affected or relocated people at all, so there is no Bank outcome figure to set against ICIJ's.
tanzania-tscp-compensation-delays.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group's review. The report notes that the project had no grievance procedure at contractor level, which could have helped document and monitor complaints by workers.
tanzania-tscp-compensation-delays.outcome: The credits closed on 26 November 2020 and the completion report rated the outcome Satisfactory, as did the Independent Evaluation Group's review. The report records that payments to contractors were also often delayed for the same shortage of counterpart funds, which delayed contract execution and brought periodic complaints to the Bank from contractors. It says the delayed availability of counterpart funds is a portfolio-wide issue affecting other Bank-financed urban projects in Tanzania as well. Whether the people whose compensation was more than nine months late were eventually paid in full is not stated.

tanzania-tscp-compensation-delays.confidence_note: This is the thinnest of the eight entries from this batch. The harm is a delay: the completion report says resettlement plan implementation was often delayed, sometimes to over nine months, when local authorities lacked funds to compensate affected people, and that this delayed construction and raised complaints. It attaches no count of people to that delay, does not say which cities the nine months applied to, does not say how many complaints were made, and does not say whether anyone went unpaid at closing. All the counts of people and structures given above are planning figures from subproject resettlement plans of March 2010, not outcomes, and the completion report publishes no outcome figure for resettlement at all. The report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review both rated the project Satisfactory and the report says the subprojects complied with the resettlement plans. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of compensation under this project was found. Only three of the project's subproject resettlement plans were examined. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date on its pages; the 22 October 2021 date is the Bank's catalogue field for the document and is unverified at document level.
tanzania-tscp-compensation-delays.conditions: The project triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. Environmental and social impact assessments, environmental and social management plans and resettlement action plans were prepared for the prioritised subprojects in each local government area, under an environmental and social management framework and a resettlement policy framework, using funds from an earlier Bank project to pay the consulting firms. Affected people were identified and compensation amounts set in line with Tanzanian law and the Bank's resettlement policy, and the plans were reviewed and monitored by the President's Office and the Bank. Paying the compensation was the local government authorities' own responsibility, as counterpart funding, and the completion report records that they repeatedly lacked the money. Grievance handling committees were set up in every subproject area, trained on a manual the President's Office wrote, and kept logbooks of complaints; the report says their activities were never budgeted at design, that there was no grievance procedure at contractor level for workers, and that their functioning after the project closed was uncertain (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 13 May 2021).

vietnam-redp-small-hydro-land.community: The credit was lent on through Vietnamese banks to developers, mostly private companies, who built 19 small hydropower plants with a combined capacity of 319.6 MW. The Bank's completion report gives the outcome in two places with two different figures. In its safeguards section it says the plants 'did not involve significant resettlement and/or create any adverse socioeconomic impacts' and that 'in total, the project required reallocation of less than 50 households and affected more than 2,000 households in term of losses of agricultural/tree crop land and sources of incomes.' In its annex it says the implementation 'did not involve significant resettlement and no adverse socioeconomic impacts have been recorded' and that 'in total, the project required reallocation of less than 50 households and approximately 2,500 households were affected in terms of loss of agricultural/tree crop land and sources of income.' Neither passage gives an exact count of households reallocated, and the two numbers of households that lost farmland and income differ by about 500 without explanation. The report says the land acquisition, compensation, livelihood restoration and ethnic minority development complied with the resettlement plans and ethnic minority development plans, that a grievance mechanism let affected households complain at village, commune and district level or directly to the developers' field offices, and that minor issues such as slightly late compensations, the carrying out of the ethnic minority plans, and reporting and documentation were identified on time and addressed by the developers. It records a footnote that the developers were responsible for all the costs related to the resettlement and normally had strong incentives to settle them. The subproject resettlement plans say something different from the completion report about relocation. The plan for the Nam Tang plant in Tram Tau district, Yen Bai province records 19 displaced households with 105 displaced persons and states 'there is no HH have to relocate', with its table giving relocated displaced persons as nil and non-relocated as 19 households. The plan for the Nam Vui plant at Phin Ngan commune, Bat Xat district, Lao Cai province counts 35 affected households across villages in the commune, two of them severely affected, again with relocated displaced persons at nil. The plan for the Phin Ho plant at Ban Khoang commune, Sa Pa district, Lao Cai province records 22 displaced households with 157 persons and states 'there is no HH have to relocate'. The plan for the Dak Me plant in Da Long commune, Dam Rong district, Lam Dong province records seven affected households whose occupied agricultural land exceeds the threshold for severe impact. The plan for the Ha Tay plant in Chu Pah district, Gia Lai province records 68 households of the Ba-na ethnic group in the Dak To Ve and Ha Tay communes. On the environmental side the report records that the project had poor environmental safeguard compliance in the first few plants during 2012 and 2013, particularly over the impacts of access roads and water channels, naming landslides and erosion, worker camp and solid waste management, worker safety and environmental flow, and that a remedy action plan with physical works by the subprojects, enhanced monitoring and supervision and safeguard training brought compliance back to moderately satisfactory from 2014. The project's own status reports rated the development objective Unsatisfactory in February 2013 and implementation progress Moderately Unsatisfactory from March 2012.
vietnam-redp-small-hydro-land.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,500 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report says the project required the reallocation of fewer than 50 households, which is a ceiling and not a count, and gives the number of households that lost agricultural or tree-crop land and sources of income as more than 2,000 in one passage and approximately 2,500 in another. No document found gives an exact count of households or people actually relocated, and the five subproject resettlement plans examined all record nil relocated displaced persons.
vietnam-redp-small-hydro-land.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group's review. The report lists worker safety among the subjects of poor environmental safeguard compliance in the first few plants during 2012 and 2013 and does not say that anyone was hurt.
vietnam-redp-small-hydro-land.outcome: The credit closed on 30 June 2018. The completion report rated the outcome Highly Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed. The report says all the completed subprojects were reported operating, that commercial banks went on to finance a further 1,500 MW of privately financed small hydropower outside the project's lending, and that there were no major pending safeguard issues, with follow-up actions required on minor ones. It records no count of how many of the households that lost farmland and income had their livelihoods restored.

vietnam-redp-small-hydro-land.confidence_note: This is one of the two thinnest of the eight entries from this batch, and the lender denies the harm in terms. The completion report states that the project did not involve significant resettlement and that no adverse socioeconomic impacts have been recorded, and rates the project Highly Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review agrees and adds that there were no large-scale resettlements. What is set out above is what the same report records beside those statements: fewer than 50 households reallocated, and more than 2,000 or approximately 2,500 households that lost agricultural or tree-crop land and sources of income. Both numbers of households are the Bank's own and the report does not explain the difference between them; the reallocation figure is a ceiling, not a count. The report names no plant, province or community in its safeguards section, so which of the 19 plants the reallocation happened at is not stated, and the five subproject resettlement plans examined all record nil relocated persons. The per-plant figures above are planning figures from those plans. No independent account of land acquisition at any of these plants was found. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date on its pages; the 1 September 2019 date is the Bank's catalogue field for the document and is unverified at document level.
vietnam-redp-small-hydro-land.conditions: The Ministry of Industry and Trade prepared a resettlement policy framework and an ethnic minority policy framework for the project, and each plant had its own environmental impact assessment, environmental management plan, resettlement plan and, where ethnic minorities were affected, an ethnic minority development plan, prepared under the project's environmental safeguard framework. The involuntary resettlement policy was triggered; the safeguard policies triggered were changed at the restructuring of 10 June 2014. Under the project's design the developers, not the state, bore all the costs of resettlement, which the completion report says gave them strong incentives to settle them. Affected households could complain at village, commune and district level or directly to a developer's field office. An independent panel of experts reviewed the subprojects at both appraisal and implementation stages (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 14 December 2018; IEG ICR Review).

rows.reason: Screened out on a sentence in a late resettlement plan, stated as an outcome. ONEE's involuntary resettlement and land acquisition plan for component TK-05, the Chichaoua to Agadir 400 kV line, says: 'Le present projet a ete realise dans des regions rurales a vocation agricole loin des habitations par consequent aucun deplacement physique d'individus n'a eu lieu' - the project was built in rural farming areas far from dwellings, so no physical displacement of individuals took place. The same plan says the tower footprints run between 49 and 100 square metres inside generally large agricultural plots, that the owners were paid both for the land ceded and for crop damage, and that they could go on farming once the works finished; for one lot 96 per cent of the land was bare grazing and for the other 95 per cent was state forest under temporary occupation orders. The appraisal document of 14 May 2008 adds that the Tamansourt and Dar Bouazza substations would not involve any land acquisition, and Dar Bouazza was later dropped. So no dwelling and no livelihood site was taken. What the completion report does record, and what a reader may wish to weigh against this drop, is that as for land acquisition and right of way, 95 per cent of private landowners and 16 per cent of collective land representatives had been compensated by November 2015, and that compensation for the remaining 52 private landowners and 48 collective land users, about US$220,000, was secured through an escrow account by project closing on 31 December 2015; the report says ONEE secured payment of all compensation related to social safeguards and paid crop loss compensation in full. One of the resettlement plans also carries as an annex the full text of a judgment ONEE obtained against the person who opposed the siting of tower number 187. The map's tangier-amendis-veolia-2015 case was checked and is a different matter, a water and power concession dispute in Tangier, not this project. A date discrepancy worth recording: the completion report's cover page is dated 29 May 2016 and its exchange-rate line 16 May 2016, while the Bank's archive date for the same document is 29 May 2018 and its filename says 22 May 2018. rows.project: Northern Corridor Transport Improvement Project, Kenya, approved 17 Jun 2004
rows.reason: The outcome is a count of people compensated, not a record of harm. The completion report of 29 June 2016 says resettlement action plans were prepared for all road work contracts and 'in total 1,055 project affected people were compensated under the NCTIP', that the national highways authority carried out land acquisition for five road sections between 2010 and 2015 for KSh 946 million 'without experiencing any substantial delays in civil works', and that the airports authority also carried out land acquisition satisfactorily for upgrading Kisumu Airport 'except one landowner who refused to move', with no outcome for that landowner given. Its summary says that for the most part compliance with environmental and social safeguards was largely satisfactory throughout, and its only adverse note is that the highways authority had not yet prepared a resettlement action plan completion report. The report does carry a table of implementation challenges under the involuntary resettlement policy - compensation of project affected people without legal rights, for example open air market traders with make-shift structures; no clear guidelines on livelihood restoration; most of the road reserves encroached upon; political interferences; and lack of adequate funds for timely resettlement plan implementation - but those are categories of difficulty, not counted events, and the report attaches no figure, place or date to any of them. The project's own resettlement plans do schedule named individuals losing kiosks, shops and houses on the road reserve, with amounts, and record that of the affected structures 65 per cent were kiosks, 20.3 per cent houses and 14.6 per cent shops in one section and 27 per cent houses in two others; those are planning documents. Searches for Kenyan press, audit or court material on compensation under this project found nothing specific to it. Documents: Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR2771 (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/722331467780143697/pdf/ICR2771-P082615-Box396252B-PUBLIC-disclosed-7-1-16.pdf); IEG ICR Review (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/772941488492989394/pdf/ICRR-Disclosable-P082615-03-02-2017-1488492975178.pdf).
